cases.name: 100 Buckout Road
cases.applicant: Nick (applicant's professional); Rick (planner covering)

timeline.summary: The board discussed 100 Buckout Road following a site walk, where the town engineer (John Kellard) suggested revisions to handle grading changes and the applicant's engineer Nick prepared a revised plan the board had not yet seen. The main procedural question was whether the wetland permit could be handled administratively as a minor permit rather than requiring Conservation Board review; the Conservation Board chair (George) confirmed by text that the sidewalk work is very minor with no need for board review. The board debated timing for a December versus January public hearing and agreed to move toward a public hearing, with a draft resolution finding the wetland permit minor and processing it administratively with town engineer input.

Reopened continued public hearing on a new residence involving steep-slope and wetland-buffer disturbance. The applicant argued that many draft resolution conditions (retaining wall, tree count, earthwork, soil testing/infiltration, silt fence) were repeat comments already addressed, and asked to be voted on tonight. The board would not approve: an SHPO/historic-cemetery notification and a tax-map-versus-survey boundary discrepancy remained open, and, most significantly, roughly an acre of wetland mitigation for about a half acre of buffer disturbance had been steered toward administrative handling by the town wetland consultant rather than the Conservation Board. The board concluded that no site directive could authorize skipping the Conservation Board, directed the applicant to prepare a full mitigation plan and route it through the Conservation Board, and to re-notice the public hearing, targeting the May meeting.

This was a continuation of a public hearing on a wetlands permit that the board had previously declined to treat as a minor permit, sending the applicant back to the Conservation Board. The Conservation Board reviewed the home mitigation plan, found the structure could not be moved out of the buffer, judged the mitigation (slightly more than 2:1) adequate, and recommended approval. The applicant also confirmed via SHIPO that the project would not impact the African American historic cemetery across the street, and a previously missing page of engineering conditions was now reflected in the draft resolution. The board closed the public hearing and approved the resolution.

cases.name: 7 Hollow Ridge Road
cases.applicant: Lauren Brennan (Alton Engineering) with property owner Charlie Catch and a landscape architect

timeline.summary: Continuation of a hearing on a single-family house with pool, patio, driveway and stormwater capture. The applicant reported reducing the disturbance area (from ~71,700 to ~62,000 sf) and tree removal (from 134 to 99). Much of the discussion centered on the town engineer's (John Kellard) memo, which had arrived late and which the applicant team had not yet seen: knoll grading, ~10-foot driveway cuts on a 14% grade, rock outcroppings, the need for a temporary sediment trap rather than just silt fence, and trench drains for driveway runoff. The board declined to adopt the resolution until the applicant reviews and addresses the memo, keeping the hearing open and adjourning. Landscaping (six white pines for rear screening) was also debated.

The resumed hearing covered erosion control, grading and drainage worked out that afternoon with town engineer John Kellard, including trench-drain sump structures, two temporary sediment basins, construction ditch relocation to the toe of slope, and possibly removing a rear retaining wall so drainage could be consolidated to the front. Roughly 22 trees may be removed and the drip-line grading impacts remain undefined. A neighbor's letter about screening was addressed via a resolution condition adding 20 green-giant arborvitae. The chair concluded the plans were too incomplete to approve and sent the applicant back to finalize drawings with the engineer before returning.

Continued public hearing on a residential site plan. The landscaping plan had been enhanced, with 21 green giant arborvitae shown in the rear versus the 20 requested, and a well permit from the Health Department was in hand. The town engineer noted that drip lines showed the tree-removal count increasing from 99 to 131 and required the site to be stabilized before framing, with those revisions on the plan. Board members had no further questions; the board closed the public hearing and adopted the site plan resolution.

cases.name: 250 East Middle Patent Road
cases.applicant: Neil and Vanessa Lucy (owners); attorney Michael Sirignano; Jerry Barrett (landscape architect) and Nicholas of Hudson Engineering

timeline.summary: A pool application first seen ~5 years ago under prior owners (the Benises) returned with the Lucy family. After a site conversation with the chair, the team presented a sketch moving the pool 16 feet back and about 4 feet lower so it sits in the side yard rather than the front yard, eliminating the zoning setback variance but still implicating the scenic road overlay, a conservation buffer, and 25% slopes. The revised concept would tie the pool to the existing bluestone patio via a retaining/engineered wall (est. 6-8 ft) with a forward sitting wall. The board strongly endorsed the new direction and asked the applicant to formalize plans with landscape and wetland mitigation plans and return.

Following a site walk the prior week, the board reviewed a revised plan that pulls the structure a full 16 feet further from the road and roughly 18 feet lower in elevation, making it essentially not visible. Members found it favorably sited and no longer in the front yard. A wetland permit is triggered because the work is within 150 feet of the wetland, and discussion clarified the steep-slope (25%) regulation, with engineer John Kellard noting the rear yard is under 25% which narrows the review. The board voted to refer the applicant to the Conservation Board, targeting a September public hearing on return.

The board struck a condition, adopted the NegDec, the site-plan resolution, and the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.

cases.name: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road
cases.address: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Michael Lair (owner); Jerry Barrett, landscape architect

timeline.summary: Reopened (re-noticed) public hearing on renovation/expansion of existing golf greens and tees, plus wetlands and tree-removal permits. The applicant removed two proposed tees, submitted a buffer/screening landscape plan (12 trees, 54 shrubs), and brought a golf pro to argue the short hole poses little errant-ball risk. Neighbors (Kalindi Bhat at 98, and Barry Edelman at 88 via counsel) pressed safety concerns about golf balls crossing property lines. timeline.status: public hearing continued | adjourned to Nov 10
timeline.summary: Continued wetlands-permit hearing for an existing golf putting green and two tee boxes. The applicant proposed a localized 10-ft-wide by 6-ft-high net above the upper tee plus deflectors to protect the neighbor. Chairman Carthy floated conceptual town legislation to regulate putting greens (treat greens as structures respecting side-yard setbacks, and limit tee distance to 3x the setback), while stressing it would not govern this application. The board pressed the applicant to pull the tees closer to the green so only chip/pitch shots are used, add netting at the road-side tee, and add evergreen screening near the OWTS; the applicant argued a 25-year no-incident history. The hearing was adjourned to Nov 10 for a revised plan and a resolution vote.

cases.name: 76 Virginia Road
cases.applicant: Tony Viziano (attorney) and Jose Rodriguez, CC Engineering, for the property owner (645/6.45 North Broadway operator)

timeline.summary: Reopened hearing on a project involving a substantial rock cut stabilized by an anchored netting system, tied to bringing the applicant's nearby office property into conformance. The applicant reported a completed Phase 1A archaeological study (no/low sensitivity, submitted to and accepted by SHPO) and the board adopted an amended negative declaration removing a mischaracterized historical-society letter reference. Major unresolved items kept the hearing open: a written seismic/vibration monitoring plan for the town engineer to review, a deeded perpetual maintenance obligation plus bonding, whether a maintenance bond also covers repair/re-pinning after a rock dislodgement, and a truck-staging/queuing plan for a project projecting ~20 trucks a day for months. Public speakers raised the NEG DEC wording and challenged anchor lengths, safety, and whether an alternate design was considered.

After roughly six weeks of work, the board closed the public hearing and adopted a conditioned site-plan resolution for a landscaping-business building requiring a large rock cut (up to ~70 feet, chipping not blasting, no on-site crushing) with a soil-nailed/netted retaining wall. Extensive discussion covered a seismic/vibration/air/noise monitoring plan with stop-work exceedance thresholds and town notifications, a truck-routing safety plan queuing trucks off-site, an annual operating permit and wall-maintenance manual traveling with the deed, and a Phase 1B archaeological survey (nothing on site; high Revolutionary-War sensitivity next door at Miller Hill). A long exchange on insurance and catastrophic-failure risk resolved into a condition requiring the owner to maintain reasonable liability/property insurance to the satisfaction of the town attorney.

timeline.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions
timeline.summary: The applicant proposed a new two-story, four-bedroom colonial (~3,000 sq ft living area, ~4,000 sq ft gross) on a vacant lot, with nearly all disturbance in the wetland buffer, municipal sewer connection, and a mitigation plan the Conservation Board had recommended (conditioned on footprint reduction and a DEC wetland permit). A neighbor's engineer (Chris Morezello, for 1615 Old Orchard) raised three concerns: whether stormwater design accounted for climate change per the 2024 DEC manual, that the house remains among the largest by building coverage in the neighborhood, and driveway sight-distance/blind-spot safety. Jane Black reiterated the Conservation Board's view that the house should be smaller and in keeping with neighbors. The board defended the plan: the driveway conforms (200-foot sight line one way plus a variance), new construction is reasonably larger, footprint/impervious coverage sit within the neighborhood range, and the ten Cultec infiltrators exceed neighboring older homes' stormwater handling. The board declined to hold the applicant to a stricter-than-code future climate standard, closed the hearing, and approved the resolution as technically amended (septic reference corrected to sewer; DEC/NYC-DEP and plan-sheet conditions added).

cases.name: Myanos River Gorge Nature Center

cases.name: 154 Lafayette Avenue (Mistis Transport - office + truck parking)

The board debated at length whether parallel (respecting the police) or perpendicular (which neighbors do under grandfathered variances) better serves the site, given early-morning (3-5am) truck turnover and a possible 'demolition derby' of drivers arriving at once. The owner spoke passionately, feeling singled out relative to neighbors who park outside. The board ultimately directed the applicant to move forward with the parallel-parking plan as presented and scheduled a public hearing, reasoning that pursuing perpendicular would require ZBA/town-board approvals and delay.

cases.name: 76 Virginia Road (rock-cut / retaining-wall project)
cases.applicant: Tony (Anthony) Vinesiano, owner; Jose Rodriguez, PE, Sessie Consulting Engineers (geotechnical)

timeline.summary: Discussion of a substantial rock-excavation and retaining-wall project. Following a prior board directive, a town geotechnical engineer (Carlin Simpson) reviewed the applicant's plans and, after 21 test pits and eight borings with geophysical scanning, reported that roughly 99% of requested data had been provided, with only anchor pull-out loads still to be translated onto the plans. The engineer described a controlled, no-blasting method (line drilling, chopping/feather splitting in 10-foot lifts, draped ring-net systems with rock anchors, vibration monitoring, existing-condition surveys within 500 feet) over a three-to-four-month timeframe. The board pressed on safety and what happens if something is 'missed,' and agreed to schedule a public hearing (targeted for December 8) with the geotechnical engineer present. Counsel raised SEQRA: the action is unlisted, a full EAF was requested, and the ZBA variance may need to be revisited because SEQRA was not completed before it.

timeline.summary: A new single-family home requiring Planning Board review for an ~11-foot (8-foot structural plus 3-foot aesthetic extension) retaining wall, on a pond-front lot with wetlands, prior-owner disturbance, and an existing pool to be reduced. The core open issue was stormwater treatment: a buried CulTec system under the courtyard versus a town-engineer-suggested bioretention/rain garden in the wetland buffer, which would require returning to the conservation board. After debating whether approving now would set a precedent for laden conditions, the board approved the current plan (site plan, wetlands permit, tree-removal permit) as amended, with the applicant expected to return for a full amendment once the rain-garden and mitigation revisions are worked out. Adam Kaufman explained the membership-club parking code offers three standards and recommended the one-space-per-200-square-feet floor-area standard (about nine spaces), which likely avoids a variance, noting the shared lot and evening-only use. Members debated whether to use the more conservative fire-code/occupancy figure (about 17-18 spaces) as a more defensible, realistic number. The board agreed to cite a standard, made a referral to the ZBA for a parking variance if necessary, and Adam agreed to run the numbers; the submitted plan already showed 18 spaces.

Adam Kaufman opened a policy discussion on how the board handles extensions of time. The board agreed to place extensions at the top of future meetings so professionals can dispatch them quickly, while a participating professional argued the published agenda order should not bind the chair (comparing it to a courtroom). Adam also proposed adding whereas clauses to extension resolutions stating whether another board (e.g., the ZBA) had a required approval and its status, so lapses are clearly documented. cases.name: 1613 Old Orchard Street

cases.summary: The applicant proposed a new two-story, four-bedroom colonial (~3,000 sq ft living area, ~4,000 sq ft gross) on a vacant lot, with nearly all disturbance in the wetland buffer, municipal sewer connection, and a mitigation plan the Conservation Board had recommended (conditioned on footprint reduction and a DEC wetland permit). cases.address: 2 Israel Townsend Hill Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Andrew Vaccarello (representing); part of 32 Wortched Drive subdivision
cases.summary: Continued public hearing on new house construction with a tree-removal permit. In response to prior direction for a 'robust planting plan,' the applicant added 12 trees (8 Arborvitae, 4 Eastern Hemlock) integrated with existing vegetation along the neighbor's property line for headlight/visual screening, and removed a rain garden to save trees. The neighbor (Darren Lampert) objected that the proposed 4-foot trees were insufficient. The Board closed the hearing and approved the site development plan and tree-removal permit, conditioned on noting the prior-day ARB approval and revising the planting schedule to 8-10 foot trees.
cases.publicComment: Darren Lampert (neighbor) said the originally proposed 4-foot trees would not screen headlights and asked for larger stock; the Board agreed and required 8-10 foot trees.

memberPositions.evidence: Agreed the four-foot trees were inadequate and directed a condition requiring 8-10 foot trees, then moved the approval as amended.
When asked to opine on tree size, agreed with the neighbor that larger (8-foot) screening trees are customary and appropriate.

cases.name: Lot 4, 32 Wortched Drive subdivision (Israel Townsend Hill)
cases.address: Lot 4, 32 Wortched Drive, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Andrew Vaccarello (representing)
cases.summary: Discussion/introduction of a proposed four-bedroom home on the 1.6-acre Lot 4, consistent with the original subdivision, with eight trees for removal, moderate-to-steep slopes, a walkout basement, two retaining walls, and a septic system under county review. The home was reoriented to face Israel Townsend Hill Road. The applicant asked to set a public hearing; the Board scheduled a site walk (next Wednesday) and agreed to notice a hearing for Oct 27.

cases.name: 18 Long Pond Road
cases.address: 18 Long Pond Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Daniel and Joanna (owners); Dean Poishler, landscape architect
cases.summary: Referral back from the Conservation Board (which was split, with only four of seven members present) on a pool, spa, and patio within a wetland buffer. The applicant reduced the pool and patio (~25-50%), increased the wetland setback from about 12 to 19-20 feet, and raised mitigation planting to three-to-one to convert a low-functioning wetland to higher-functioning. Conservation liaison Jane Black explained the split: two members found the property would be improved by the mitigation, while dissenters objected over a culvert/former stream location and the small backyard size. The Board was favorable, viewing it as a net positive for the wetland and a reasonable suburban amenity, and directed that a public hearing be scheduled (in November).
cases.publicComment: Jane Black (Conservation Board liaison) reported the board's split decision; the homeowner and applicant described the culvert/pipe and mitigation improvements.

memberPositions.evidence: Having visited the site, called it a very tight improvement that would leave the wetland enhanced (net positive), said the Board hasn't opposed recreational uses in wetland buffers, and was hard-pressed to deprive residents of amenities they value in suburbia.

Agreed with the engineer's assessment that stormwater will be captured and the wetland enhancements are a positive for the project, asking only that the applicant protect and maintain the plastic culvert pipe during construction.

cases.name: 1/11 Round Hill (driveway field change)
cases.address: Round Hill area, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: (existing subdivision lot)
cases.summary: The town engineer presented a minor field change shifting a driveway slightly back into the site to create a high point at elevation 90 and better tie in a bridge, with no additional disturbance and remaining within the easement. The Board opened and approved the field change by motion.

themes.note: Dominant at 12 Seymour Place East; runoff, failing infiltration, and street flooding drove a site walk.
Core dispute at 92 & 94 Round Hill Road; Ruisi opposed, Carthy skeptical of the risk.
18 Long Pond pool mitigation viewed as net positive; also implicated at 92/94 Round Hill.
Screening buffers at 2 Israel Townsend Hill and 92/94 Round Hill; 8-10 foot trees required.
RPRC appeal resolved with a one-third progress report to the planner.
Ruisi and Sauro wary of revisiting sealed/final approvals in the Toll appeal.

staffInput.summary: Gave background on the RPRC appeal and the ARB's color-scheme/landscaping concerns, noting the landscape and color schemes were already ARB-approved; managed plan references and hearing logistics throughout, and would take the applicant's one-third report and coordinate notices.

Provided extensive drainage analysis at 12 Seymour Place East (swale integrity, infiltration outflow, and diverting proposed stormwater toward Tripling Lane) and agreed to a site walk; assessed the 18 Long Pond culvert and mitigation favorably; and presented and endorsed the 111 Round Hill driveway field change.

Referenced only - the chair noted a conversation with Vincent between meetings; the Conservation Board's split recommendation on 18 Long Pond was presented in person by board member Jane Black rather than DeAnno.

meetings.attributionNote: Only three members were present and all were clearly identifiable: Christopher Carthy (presiding chair, the dominant voice), Steven Sauro (repeatedly addressed as 'Steve,' attending virtually - the objector's reference to 'member Sorrow' wanting netting at the prior meeting is an ASR mangling that confirms Sauro), and Lawrence Ruisi (ASR 'Ruizi,' addressed as 'Larry,' who read hearing notices and made several motions). meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Planning Board approved the Oct 16 minutes and handled a full agenda: it opened and closed a public hearing and approved the Lot 4 house at 1 Israel Townsend Hill; continued the contentious 92 & 94 Round Hill Road wetlands/golf putting-green hearing (adjourned to Nov 10 pending revised safety plans); closed and approved 12 Seymour Place East with a drainage condition delegated to the town engineer; scheduled a public hearing for 428-436 Main Street; and discussed still-evolving site plans for 2 & 4 Massaro Court (retaining walls) and 4 Kensico Court (Awesome Landscaping parking/outdoor storage). meetings.durationNote: Chairman Carthy presided; members Steven Sauro (Steve), Michael Pollack (Michael), and Lawrence Ruisi (Larry) were clearly identifiable and active. Quorum present. Thomas Crispi could not be positively identified as speaking this meeting.

cases.name: 1 Israel Townsend Hill (Lot 4, 32 Orchard Drive Subdivision)
cases.address: 1 Israel Townsend Hill, North Castle, NY (Tax Lot 108.01-6-1.4, R1A)
cases.applicant: Andrew Vekarello for 32 Orchard Drive R-Monk LLC
cases.summary: Second/new single-family house on Lot 4 of the previously approved (2024) 32 Orchard Drive subdivision. The applicant proposed removing eight trees, two front retaining walls, a walkout, a septic system and well consistent with the approved IPP, directing stormwater to the shared BMP across Israel Townsend Hill. The home was slightly reoriented from the subdivision layout to align with the new street and reduce excavation/retaining walls. ARB approval was obtained Oct 15 with only minor landscaping comments; the board opened the hearing, took brief questions, closed it, and adopted the resolution.
cases.publicComment: No neighbors or members of the public appeared for this application.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked Adam about the side of the house being 'very present from Orchard' and the line of sight, and questioned the driveway slope (~10%) and the front-only foundation plantings, but was satisfied the remaining mature trees screen the lot.

cases.name: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road
cases.address: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Adam Wexton (attorney), Tim Allen (engineer) and Jerry Barrett (landscape architect) for owner Mr. Edelman
cases.status: public hearing continued | adjourned to Nov 10
cases.summary: Continued wetlands-permit hearing for an existing golf putting green and two tee boxes. The applicant proposed a localized 10-ft-wide by 6-ft-high net above the upper tee plus deflectors to protect the neighbor. Chairman Carthy floated conceptual town legislation to regulate putting greens (treat greens as structures respecting side-yard setbacks, and limit tee distance to 3x the setback), while stressing it would not govern this application. The board pressed the applicant to pull the tees closer to the green so only chip/pitch shots are used, add netting at the road-side tee, and add evergreen screening near the OWTS; the applicant argued a 25-year no-incident history. The hearing was adjourned to Nov 10 for a revised plan and a resolution vote.
cases.publicComment: Judson C. of Keane & Beane, PC appeared for neighbor Mr. Edelman: no issue with 94 Round Hill, but for 92 urged netting at BOTH tees, plus additional planting or a compliant six-foot fence behind the green; wanted to see a revised plan before any adjournment vote. Tone: cooperative but insistent on stronger protection.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he is concerned about BOTH tees, that a full wedge swing from 70 yards will send errant balls into the neighbor's yard 16 feet off the property line, and that he wants to walk his backyard 'without getting smacked in the head with a golf ball'; agreed pulling tees closer would substantially reduce his concern.

Proposed the tee-distance legislation concept and repeatedly pushed the applicant to pull tees closer to the green so only a chip/pitch swing is needed; noted the board would be 'setting a precedent' approving this on a site plan and set a firm Nov 10 vote.

Called the proposed legislation 'a little too onerous' and 'too aggressive to start dictating distances of golf teas,' favoring instead moving the green inland; constructively suggested a zigzag row of evergreens near the tee/OWTS and that any netting be black to disappear.

Emphasized there is an established prior approval history and that concerns center on neighbor safety; favored safety measures 'at the area of the target,' was open to netting at the green, and questioned whether an 8-10 ft net would catch the more dangerous bladed/scalded shots.

cases.name: 12 Seymour Place East
cases.address: 12 Seymour Place East, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Applicant team with project engineer Ralph
cases.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions
cases.summary: Reopened hearing focused on cul-de-sac drainage. Following a site walk with town engineer John Kellard, the applicant split the drainage systems so the new garage has its own dedicated infiltration system (both designed to hold up to a 100-year storm with zero discharge), added a trench drain at the driveway bottom tied to the town culvert, converted lawn to planted meadow, and will confirm/repair the existing overflow pipe to the town system. The board closed the hearing and adopted the (date-amended) resolution, with the standing stormwater-mitigation condition delegated to the town engineer administratively.
cases.publicComment: No neighbors spoke; the chair re-explained the drainage benefits for the public record.

memberPositions.evidence: Expressed confidence in the town engineer's ability to police the drainage condition administratively and moved to close the hearing and adopt the resolution as amended.

cases.name: 428-436 Main Street
cases.applicant: Charles Marteban (attorney) for 428-436 Main Street LLC / George Calcutini
cases.summary: Largely procedural update to a site plan approved in January 2025. The prior approval was conditioned on providing parking for an accessory apartment; the ZBA later granted a variance for 22 parking spaces, so the site plan must be updated to match. The board declined to skip the required (now-expired) public hearing and scheduled a new hearing, with a resolution expected at the next meeting.

cases.name: 2 & 4 Massaro Court
cases.applicant: Nicholas Shari, Hudson Engineering & Consulting
cases.summary: Two proposed two-family dwellings on the first two lots of a recently approved three-lot subdivision. Much of the driveway, utilities and stormwater remain unchanged from the subdivision plans; updates add the buildings and elevated decks (at-grade rear terraces to be removed). Outstanding items include structural plans and protective barriers for tall retaining walls, a driveway revision to add a required parking space per unit, and a possible gross land coverage variance the applicant expects to avoid by converting a turnaround area to parking. Chairman Carthy strongly pressed for tiered, more attractive retaining walls (some near 10-11 ft) rather than a single tall wall. No hearing yet; revised plans to follow.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly challenged the applicant to redesign the ~10-ft straight retaining walls into a tiered, landscaped system that looks attractive on a residential lot, recalling a Harrison wall that made him think 'this town needs a planning board,' and doubted the plans would be ready for the next meeting.

cases.name: 4 Kensico Court (Awesome Landscaping)
cases.applicant: John G. Scarlett Jr. for Awesome Landscaping
cases.summary: Proposed reuse of an existing building for a small (~150 sq ft) office plus truck parking and outdoor storage for a landscaping business. Review letter issues include lighting, some existing parking spaces sitting on town property, and 20-ft aisles that fall short of the 24-ft standard. The board discussed reworking the ~51-space lot to become code-compliant (or seeking targeted ZBA variances) while preserving impervious coverage and truck turnaround. The chair was supportive of the concept and directed the applicant to produce the best compliant site plan possible before any variance request.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he has no problem with the office-to-parking relationship and called it 'an awesome idea' to reuse the space, urging the applicant to do what is needed to make the plan work and comply with the town code before going to the ZBA.

cases.name: 22 Whipple Road East (Extension of Time)
cases.address: 22 Whipple Road East, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented via correspondence; not present initially)
cases.summary: Request to extend a site plan approval whose conditions (an easement to the town attorney's satisfaction and a revised evergreen-screening landscaping plan) remain unfulfilled. A neighbor's attorney letter recited a history of stop-work orders and non-compliance and asked the board to hold the applicant's feet to the fire. Rather than the default one-year extension, the board granted a shorter extension to Feb 7, 2026, to require the applicant to submit the easement and landscaping paperwork; planting itself is enforced later by the building department at CO.
cases.publicComment: Neighbor Stephen McLaughlin (24 Whipple Road East) spoke, concerned about repeated delays, wanting the screening done at the optimal spring time and a quality (not 'rough shot') planting rather than more slippage. Tone: frustrated but engaged.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised that the planting window is closing and material is limited this time of year, but did not want to preclude the applicant from finishing; supported a shorter extension to keep pressure on.
Helped work through the timeline, noting the resolution is satisfied once the paperwork/easement is submitted and settling on the end-of-February deadline.

cases.name: Summit Golf Club (Extensions of Time)

cases.applicant: Summit Golf Club (Sal; water system designed by Mike Schrodtell)
cases.status: extensions of time granted (site plan and 8th/final subdivision 90-day)

cases.name: 448 Bedford Road (Extension of Time)
cases.applicant: Church (additional nursery-school classrooms)
cases.summary: Routine extension of time for a church's previously approved additional classrooms for its nursery school. Granted without discussion.

cases.name: 73 Whipple Road Subdivision
cases.applicant: O'Dmarzo Site Engineering and Alex Gusky for Wellness Estates LLC
cases.summary: Conditions-review for a subdivision where the hearing had been closed but too many conditions remained. Working with the engineering department, the applicant reduced the preliminary plat conditions from 15 to 3 and the final subdivision conditions from 21 to 10, all remaining items being tasks to complete rather than plan changes. The board adopted the NEG DEC and both the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.

themes.note: Dominated the Round Hill Road hearing; board split between safety concern and respecting a 25-year existing use.
Central to Seymour Place East (resolved favorably) and present in Massaro Court and Kensico Court.
Carthy pushed hard for tiered, attractive walls at 2 & 4 Massaro Court.
Screening a recurring mitigation ask at Round Hill Road and an unmet condition at 22 Whipple Road East.
Aisle width and space counts at Kensico Court and Massaro Court; parking-variance update at Main Street.
Multiple routine extensions (Whipple East, Summit, 448 Bedford) and subdivision condition sign-offs (73 Whipple).
Wetland buffer constrained relocating the Round Hill green/tees; drainage flows toward wetlands at Seymour Place East.
Eight-tree removal and steep-slope-driven layout at 1 Israel Townsend Hill, accepted.

staffInput.summary: Confirmed the 1 Israel Townsend Hill plan conforms to the approved IPP with no significant concerns; guided procedure on the Main Street public hearing, the Seymour Place resolution amendment, submission deadlines, and the mechanics of the 22 Whipple Road East extension of time.

Praised the Israel Townsend Hill plans and noted the house shift reduced excavation and retaining walls; walked the Seymour Place East site, endorsed the split 100-year drainage systems and trench drain, and was delegated to police that condition administratively; flagged the existing stormwater/culvert issues driving the neighbor's concern.

meetings.durationNote: Special meeting. New member Thomas Crispi introduced and seated (abstained on the prior Oct 27 minutes). Michael Pollack participated by phone. cases.name: 825 North Broadway (BP gas station renovation)
cases.address: 825 North Broadway, North Castle, NY (CB Zoning District, lot 122.12-4-26)
cases.applicant: Jim Gibbons, Gibbons & Gibbons (attorney), with project engineer
cases.summary: Public hearing on a site-plan application to renovate the interior, replace fuel pumps and underground storage tanks, rebuild the convenience store with a gable roof, and improve circulation, lighting, retaining walls and stormwater. No members of the public appeared. The board focused on a pump-queuing/circulation problem (cars stacking at the three in-line pumps blocking one another) and whether a 'pull forward' sign or full-service operation could mitigate it; the applicant agreed to raise full service with the owner. Rather than adopt the draft resolution, the board closed the hearing and sent the applicant home to satisfy the many open conditions (stormwater calcs for the 25-year event, upsized pipes to 8-inch minimum, ARB stone-pillar condition) and return with a tightened, near-final resolution before the building department stage.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public appeared for this application.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed the pump-queuing problem repeatedly and floated a 'please pull forward' sign, worrying a car in the lead spot ties up all three pump lanes and a car waiting would block the drive; wanted to know how the applicant could ameliorate it since 'this is our one shot at the site plan.'

Took a pragmatic view: 'you see this in so many gas spaces... you pull out of the way until the space opens up... I don't know that you can really fix it here,' treating the circulation issue as common and not a reason to hold up the project.
Deliberated on the circulation issue and full-service vs self-service; chair thanked 'Steve' for his comments. Engaged but did not object to the project.

Comfortable with the site but wanted the applicant to tighten the resolution and clear the open conditions before returning, noting pressing the applicant back before the board ensures conditions are finished before the building department; framed it as being 'close to public hearing.'

cases.name: 126 Lafayette Avenue (NC Auto Repair - solar + 3-bay addition)
cases.address: 126 Lafayette Avenue, North Castle, NY (ID Industrial District, lot 122.12-1-7)
cases.applicant: Jamie Glover, Green Hybrid Energy Solutions, for owner Elio (auto repair shop)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a site plan to legitimize the existing auto-repair use, add a 48-panel rooftop solar system and a three-bay rear addition, and remove a deteriorated Butler building and cargo trailer. No public appeared. Discussion covered the low-profile roof-mounted panels (nine inches above the roofline), the absence of a parapet wall (the adjacent Bell & Tony building screens it), and stormwater: the engineer noted no existing runoff treatment and required capture/treatment of roof-drain and paved-area runoff to the town engineer's satisfaction. The board opened and closed the hearing and adopted the draft resolution the same night, approving the application with the stormwater condition.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public appeared for this application.

memberPositions.evidence: Reviewed the resolution and raised the stormwater-quality-device condition, asking the engineer to explain treatment for parking-area/vehicle-bay runoff; satisfied once capture-and-treatment to the town engineer's satisfaction was confirmed as a condition.

Knowledgeably explained what a parapet wall is and why one is unnecessary here since the adjacent Bell & Tony building acts as a screen; treated the application as sufficient ('I think this is very sufficient').
Asked Steve to explain what a parapet wall is; engaged constructively without objection.
Moved the hearing to close and to adopt the resolution, congratulating the applicant; noted 'no good deed goes unpunished' but that the added bays were a good outcome.

cases.name: 154 Lafayette Avenue (Mistis Transport - office + truck parking)
cases.applicant: Mistis Transport (US mail contractor); Mark Herring, representative, with the owner
cases.summary: Discussion of a plan to establish an office, merge lots/move a lot line, and store US-mail delivery trucks. The applicant originally proposed perpendicular parking partly in the right-of-way, but the police department recommended against it and the town code prohibits it; the applicant returned with six parallel spaces. The board debated at length whether parallel (respecting the police) or perpendicular (which neighbors do under grandfathered variances) better serves the site, given early-morning (3-5am) truck turnover and a possible 'demolition derby' of drivers arriving at once. The owner spoke passionately, feeling singled out relative to neighbors who park outside. The board ultimately directed the applicant to move forward with the parallel-parking plan as presented and scheduled a public hearing, reasoning that pursuing perpendicular would require ZBA/town-board approvals and delay.
cases.publicComment: The owner spoke at length and emotionally, arguing his neighbors all park outside, questioning whether he was being singled out (referencing being the only Hispanic owner on the lot), and repeatedly stating he just wanted the most expeditious, workable solution.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised as making a 'very good point'; argued the perpendicular parking is not really disruptive to the street and could facilitate the building's use, and personally said he was comfortable with perpendicular, while acknowledging he saw it both ways and that pursuing it would slow the applicant.

Leaned toward respecting the police: 'when you get a request from the police department and there's an alternative way to respect that request, that's the way I would lean'; also flagged that any approval travels with the land beyond the current 3-5am operation.

Agreed with Larry, noting the approval is 'in perpetuity' and 'we don't know what that area is going to be tomorrow'; earlier said if parking travels with the building the parallel plan is the fastest path, avoiding special-use permits that would delay the applicant.

Said he saw it both ways and acknowledged 'muddying the waters,' but ultimately sided with Larry and Tom, directing the applicant to move forward with the parallel-parking plan and schedule the hearing.
Participating by phone; polled during the discussion but no substantive position was captured.

cases.name: 76 Virginia Road (rock-cut / retaining-wall project)
cases.applicant: Tony (Anthony) Vinesiano, owner; Jose Rodriguez, PE, Sessie Consulting Engineers (geotechnical)
cases.summary: Discussion of a substantial rock-excavation and retaining-wall project. Following a prior board directive, a town geotechnical engineer (Carlin Simpson) reviewed the applicant's plans and, after 21 test pits and eight borings with geophysical scanning, reported that roughly 99% of requested data had been provided, with only anchor pull-out loads still to be translated onto the plans. The engineer described a controlled, no-blasting method (line drilling, chopping/feather splitting in 10-foot lifts, draped ring-net systems with rock anchors, vibration monitoring, existing-condition surveys within 500 feet) over a three-to-four-month timeframe. The board pressed on safety and what happens if something is 'missed,' and agreed to schedule a public hearing (targeted for December 8) with the geotechnical engineer present. Counsel raised SEQRA: the action is unlisted, a full EAF was requested, and the ZBA variance may need to be revisited because SEQRA was not completed before it.
cases.publicComment: No public spoke at this discussion (Miller Park-area residents had attended a prior meeting); neighbor input is anticipated at the scheduled public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked pointed safety questions - 'how many of these situations has something got amiss?' and whether a project has ever had to be stopped - and probed ongoing field monitoring and whether adjustments during construction must be reviewed by the town's expert.

Moved the project toward a public hearing with the geotechnical engineer present, and asked whether the town's expert should check in on the project periodically 'like an architect' during construction; treated the submission as thorough and close to hearing-ready.

cases.name: 100 Buck Out Road (new house on existing lot)
cases.address: 100 Buck Out Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Malik Samad, owner/applicant; Nicholas Shariah, Hudson Engineering; John Scarlato, architect
cases.summary: Discussion of a proposed 3,700 sq ft new house replacing an existing dwelling on a lot with a cottage that will remain, referred by the RPRC to both the Planning Board and Conservation Board for steep-slope, wetland-buffer and grading impacts. The engineer corrected the plan to show two trees removed (not seven), described disturbing roughly 10,830 sq ft of steep slopes (largely bare rock outcroppings) and noted nearly all work sits within the wetland buffer, with the septic location constrained by the health department. To reduce impact, the applicant offered to eliminate a walk-out basement door and cut rock removal from about 12 feet to 4-5 feet near the wetlands. The board scheduled a joint site walk for November 19 at 8:30am and referred the application to the Conservation Board for concurrent review.

memberPositions.evidence: Welcomed the applicant's offer to reduce rock removal and eliminate the walk-out door as 'positive changes,' and directed a joint Planning/Conservation Board site walk to get a feel for the site before further review.
Consulted on scheduling the November 19 site-walk date; no substantive stance on the merits.

cases.name: 258 East Middle Patent Road (Matthews accessory dwelling / barn)
cases.address: 258 East Middle Patent Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Carol Matthews, owner; Alan Bill, JLP Engineering
cases.summary: Discussion of an accessory dwelling unit in a barn/garage building, before the board for a wetland permit, scenic-road frontage and a special permit. The applicant reported that after an October site walk and a follow-up meeting the Conservation Board was satisfied with the wetland permit and mitigation, with buffer impacts reduced from over 2,400 sq ft to 1,514 sq ft (about 70 sq ft for a handicap ramp plus stormwater and a relocated rain garden). Invasive species (Oriental bittersweet, mugwort, multiflora rose) would be removed and a mitigation planting plan provided; percolation testing was to be witnessed by the town engineer. The board found the application strong and scheduled the public hearing (targeted for the December meeting, ultimately the 24th) with a draft resolution to follow.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'a really good application' and moved to schedule the public hearing with a draft resolution ready for the next meeting.

cases.name: 40 High Street (extension of time)
cases.summary: The board granted a requested extension of time, attributed to ongoing health department (septic) issues. Handled quickly by motion and unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road (extension of time)
cases.address: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road, North Castle, NY
cases.summary: The board granted a requested extension of time, with staff noting resolution of the outstanding matter was imminent. Steven Sauro seconded the motion, which passed by unanimous voice vote.

themes.note: Dominant at 154 Lafayette (perpendicular vs parallel, police recommendation) and the pump-queuing problem at 825 North Broadway.
Central to both public hearings (825 North Broadway, 126 Lafayette) - upsized pipes, 25-year calcs, runoff treatment to town engineer's satisfaction.
Drove the 100 Buck Out Road and 258 East Middle Patent Road discussions; mitigation and buffer-impact reduction viewed favorably.
Key to 76 Virginia Road (geotech rock cut) and 100 Buck Out Road (rock outcroppings, reduced excavation).
Stone pillars at 825 North Broadway and parapet-wall/solar low profile at 126 Lafayette.
At 154 Lafayette the board weighed deferring to police against its own big-picture judgment.
Counsel flagged unlisted action, full EAF and a possible ZBA revisit for 76 Virginia Road.

Engineering/stormwater review: at 825 North Broadway noted stormwater is the biggest open concern but nothing that should hold up the site plan (25-year calcs, upsized 8-inch pipes); at 126 Lafayette confirmed no existing runoff treatment and required capture and treatment of roof-drain/paved-area runoff to the town engineer's satisfaction. Note: a consulting engineer referred to on the record as 'Rick' delivered some of these stormwater comments and may be a distinct associate rather than John Kellard.

Present from the Conservation Board for the wetland-related items; the Conservation Board (with his involvement) was reported satisfied with the 258 East Middle Patent Road wetland permit and mitigation after an October site walk, and 100 Buck Out Road was referred to the Conservation Board for concurrent wetland-buffer review.

meetings.attributionNote: The chair (Christopher Carthy) presides and speaks most; Steven Sauro (Steve), Lawrence Ruisi (Larry) and new member Thomas Crispi (Tom) were each directly addressed by name and could be attributed with reasonable confidence, especially in the 154 Lafayette parking debate and the 825 North Broadway circulation discussion. Michael Pollack participated by phone and was polled but gave little captured substance (low confidence). One board member was noted absent during deliberations. meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Planning Board held its November 24, 2025 meeting, opening and closing public hearings and approving three applications: the 10 & 20 Round Hill Way site plans (a re-approval of previously expired resolutions), the 18 Long Pond Road pool/wetlands permit, and the 258 East Middle Patten Road accessory apartment/barn. The board also granted extensions of time for Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive) and 8 Cold Drive, and held informal discussions on several matters headed to future public hearings (60 Cox Avenue/Breezemont overflow parking, the Orchard Hill subdivision access change, a Keskil Court parking-lot restriping, and 100 Buckout Road). The 92 & 94 Round Hill Road hearing was moved off the agenda. The board then adjourned into executive session for legal counsel before closing.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; motions repeatedly passed with a full board and one item noted as passing 'five ayes'. Executive session held mid-meeting for advice of counsel.

cases.name: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road
cases.summary: The chair announced at the outset that the public hearing for 92 & 94 Round Hill Road had been moved off the agenda for the evening and would be covered on another night. No substantive discussion occurred. The board confirmed whether anyone in the audience was present for the item before moving on.

cases.name: 10 & 20 Round Hill Way
cases.summary: The board opened and closed a public hearing on the 10 and 20 Round Hill Way site plans, steep slope permits and tree removal permits, then adopted draft resolutions for each lot. This was essentially a re-approval: the applications had been approved before as part of a subdivision and two site plans, but due to a miscommunication the site-plan resolutions expired and the plans were never signed, so they had to be re-submitted with prior field changes incorporated. A board member questioned how Lot 5 gets access, confirming a common driveway serves the lots off Round Hill via an easement reflected in the resolution. The board was satisfied and adopted both resolutions.

memberPositions.evidence: Read the public hearing notice for the 10 & 20 Round Hill Way applications ('Thank you, Larry').

A non-chair member pressed on how Lot 5 gets access ('it looks like lot five is getting access from Green Valley Road... how is lot five getting access?') and confirmed the common driveway and easement, then thanked the applicant for clarifying; attribution to Pollack is tentative.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive)
cases.applicant: Eagle Ridge (represented by applicant's attorney on behalf of Cory)
cases.summary: The applicant's attorney requested an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge subdivision and site plan. The subdivision plat is still with the county Department of Health for execution, but all other outstanding items (easements, etc.) have been completed, with the DOH being the only hold-up; completion is hoped for by spring 2026. The board had no questions and approved both the subdivision extension and the site plan extension.

cases.name: 8 Cold Drive
cases.applicant: Applicant's attorney (on behalf of Cory)
cases.summary: The same attorney reported on 8 Cold Drive, noting the applicant pulled the clearing and grading permit for the sport court and anticipates constructing it in spring. The board granted the requested extension of time without objection.

cases.name: 18 Long Pond Road
cases.applicant: Daniel and Joanna Novick (owners); Dean Pushlar, landscape architect
cases.summary: The board opened and closed a public hearing on a swimming pool, patio, deck modification, tree removal and landscaping within a regulated wetland buffer, ultimately approving the site plan, wetlands permit and tree removal permit. The landscape architect described a stormwater plan storing pool drawdown with slow release, an extensive planting plan providing 3x mitigation, elimination of pesticides, and habitat features; diseased beech trees would be removed. The Conservation Board deadlocked 2-2, with the town engineer explaining both sides: some members opposed 'rewarding' new disturbance on a site with a decades-old buried water course, while others saw the mitigation as a net improvement to a low-functioning wetland. The board examined topography, whether the existing 60+ year-old pipe still functions, and read a neighbor's email opposing the project despite the mitigation explanation.
cases.publicComment: Neighbor Ms. Blumenthal (50 Bankswell Road) submitted an email and spoke by phone with the chair; she raised reasonable questions about where pool water would go and, despite the detention/mitigation explanation, remained opposed to the application. The chair characterized her opposition as fair.

memberPositions.evidence: Read the public hearing notice ('Thank you, Tom') and engaged on whether the current owners were responsible for the old disturbance, agreeing it was a totally different applicant ('And Tom, I actually agree with you... totally different applicants').

Asked whether the members who voted against still agreed the mitigation improves the overall wetlands ('the mitigation that's being done today improves the overall wetlands on the property?'), an inquiry the engineer praised as 'an excellent question, Larry.'
Made the motion to approve the site plan, wetlands and tree removal permit for the 18 Long Pond Road pool ('Thank you, Steve').

Presided, probed the topography and water migration to the rear wetland, invited the engineer to explain the Conservation Board split, and read/relayed the opposing neighbor's email while treating her continued opposition as fair.

cases.name: Matthews Accessory Apartment/Barn (258 East Middle Patten Road)
cases.applicant: Matthews (owners); Alan Pilch, engineer (represented the application)
cases.summary: The board opened and closed a public hearing and approved the site plan for a detached accessory apartment (over 800 sq ft) in a renovated garage/barn to accommodate an owner's mobility needs, including a wheelchair-accessible ramp, new septic for the barn, and stormwater/rain garden improvements. The engineer reported no direct wetland impacts, minor wetland-buffer impacts offset by invasive removal and native plantings, and successful percolation testing. Members debated resolution conditions at length: whether the building-permit trigger tied to Department of Health approval should be relaxed given DOH delays, the redundant existing-septic review condition, and a weekly stormwater-inspection reporting requirement (condition 10) the applicant felt was onerous. The board kept the DOH condition intact but clarified the septic language applies to the barn, and approved the site plan.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public were present for this application.

memberPositions.evidence: Read the public hearing notice ('Thank you, Steve') and made the motion to approve; the secretary confirmed 'Steve made the motion, Tom seconding, with five ayes.'
Seconded the motion to approve the site plan, per the secretary's confirmation that 'Steve made the motion, Tom seconding, with five ayes.'

Pressed on resolution conditions in detail, questioning the weekly qualified-professional stormwater inspection requirement (condition 10) as onerous for a site outside the NYC watershed, and the redundant existing-septic review language, while ultimately supporting approval.

Presided and worked through the applicant's request to soften the DOH building-permit condition, declining to modify the resolution for one applicant while clarifying the septic language could be read as applying to the barn.

cases.name: Breezemont Day Camp (60 Cox Avenue)
cases.applicant: Breezemont (Walter, on behalf of the camp)
cases.summary: The board discussed a proposed site plan amendment to formalize on-site overflow parking for special events and staff training days at the Breezemont camp, prompted by the building department. The applicant emphasized nothing changes for the regular camp season, when hundreds of attendees are still shuttled in by bus, and the extra spaces would be used only a few days a year. Members raised concerns about spaces directly on Cox Avenue being visible and unscreened, and asked that the newly added spaces be clearly marked in color on a revised map so they can be distinguished from previously approved spaces. The matter will proceed to a noticed public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Voiced concern that the spaces directly on Cox Avenue are unscreened and 'right in your face' ('I'm concerned that the spaces on Cox are really on [display]'), distinguishing them from the better-screened westerly spaces.

Asked that the applicant's professional identify the newly added spaces in a distinct color on the map so the additions could be clearly seen ('would you ask your professional to identify the new [spaces] in a color').

cases.name: Orchard Hill Subdivision - existing house access (3 Israel Council Lane vicinity)
cases.summary: The board reviewed a straightforward change to the access configuration for the existing house within the Orchard Hill five-lot subdivision, where the current lot is bifurcated by a driveway serving a back lot. Two of the new houses have been added and two rear lots remain to come before the board. The item will proceed to a public hearing with neighbor notification by first-class mail and proof of mailing. A member cautioned that because the house is shifting slightly, the 250-foot neighbor notification list should be regenerated rather than reusing old labels.

memberPositions.evidence: Cautioned that shifting the house could change the 250-foot notification radius and that the neighbor mailing labels should be regenerated rather than reused ('be careful not to use the same label... it may change').

cases.name: Keskil Court parking lot restriping
cases.applicant: John Scarlato Jr., architect
cases.summary: The board reviewed a revised plan for a parking lot where some spaces had encroached on town/road right-of-way. The applicant eliminated the off-property spaces (they cannot be counted and may need physical removal if the highway department requires it) and restriped the existing lot, converting some aisles to one-way angled parking, yielding 41 spaces against a 30-space requirement. One outstanding item is a lighting plan for the area, which the applicant has engaged someone to prepare. The board praised the 'clever design' and will schedule a public hearing once the paperwork and notice are ready.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the 16 feet on the diagonal parking was adequate; the architect said it could even be 12 feet.

cases.name: 100 Buckout Road
cases.applicant: Nick (applicant's professional); Rick (planner covering)
cases.summary: The board discussed 100 Buckout Road following a site walk, where the town engineer (John Kellard) suggested revisions to handle grading changes and the applicant's engineer Nick prepared a revised plan the board had not yet seen. The main procedural question was whether the wetland permit could be handled administratively as a minor permit rather than requiring Conservation Board review; the Conservation Board chair (George) confirmed by text that the sidewalk work is very minor with no need for board review. The board debated timing for a December versus January public hearing and agreed to move toward a public hearing, with a draft resolution finding the wetland permit minor and processing it administratively with town engineer input.

Visibility of Cox Avenue parking and one opposing neighbor at 18 Long Pond Road.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Planning Board's final 2025 meeting was dominated by a continued public hearing on 76 Virginia Road, a proposed warehouse/office building requiring extensive rock excavation and slope stabilization beside historic Miller Hill Park, which drew heavy public opposition on safety, historic-preservation, and infrastructure grounds before being adjourned to January 26, 2026. The board also re-approved the Kent Place/Verizon parking subdivision, approved a field change at the Toll/airport-campus water tank (113 King Street), granted extensions of time on two projects, closed the 4 Vincent Lane wetlands hearing (pending ARB), and held working discussions on several single-family grading applications. It closed by voting to recommend the Town Board amend its EV-charging law to allow Level 3 chargers at IBM.
meetings.durationNote: Full five-member board present and individually identifiable (Carthy chairing; Sauro, Pollack, Crispi, and Ruisi each named in roll-call notice reads and deliberation); no absences noted. Final Planning Board meeting of 2025.

cases.name: 76 Virginia Road (National Long/Spray Sprinklers)
cases.address: 76 (78/74/56) Virginia Road, North White Plains; IND-A zoning district
cases.applicant: John Luciano / National Long Sprinklers; attorney Anthony 'Tony' Vinesiano (Venetano), architect Ron Horenyo, engineer Jose Rodriguez
cases.summary: The applicant presented a reduced 15,000 sq ft flex warehouse/office (FAR variance already granted) requiring a large six-on-one rock cut with soil nails, rock anchors, and steel mesh netting on a steep slope 12-15 feet from Miller Hill Park, a Revolutionary War battlefield. The applicant's geotechnical team and the town-retained peer reviewer, Bob Simpson (Carlin Simpson Associates), testified the design is achievable with only minor open technical items and confirmed no blasting is proposed. Extensive public comment opposed or questioned the project on catastrophic-slope-failure risk, historic preservation, water/sewer capacity, dust, truck logistics, and long-term (50+ year) maintenance liability, and Open Space chair Carrie Kayza detailed alleged misrepresentations in the applicant's environmental assessment form (SHPO consultation, air pollutants, critical environmental area). The board secured the applicant's consent to a no-blasting condition on the site plan and adjourned the hearing to gather more on the EAF, construction oversight, and a maintenance covenant/deed restriction.
cases.publicComment: Heavy and predominantly negative: residents George Keller (child safety at the cut, brown/sediment-laden well water and overtaxed century-old sewer), Kate Hall (fear of catastrophic slope failure onto the only untouched Revolutionary War battlefield in Westchester), Bonnie Fite (fear of an abandoned unfinished 'eyesore'), Doug Manston, Nora, and a powerful preservation plea from Cynthia Abbott-Coffman and Open Space chair Carrie Kayza (EAF deficiencies, SHPO not consulted, misquoted county/historical-society letters). Applicant repeatedly conceded points (no blasting, insurance, surveys, maintenance covenant).

memberPositions.evidence: Defended the applicant's legal right to develop and the town's peer-review process ('the planning board is charged with protecting...'), drove the no-blasting condition onto the site plan, but candidly played devil's advocate that the board has no good answer to the public's 20-50-year maintenance/safety question 'not just tonight but for a lot of applications.'

Pressed on who approves in-field design changes and how Simpson stays involved during construction; skeptical that two trucks on site handle ~2,000 truckloads; and stressed protecting the site 'in perpetuity' since the wall needs constant maintenance and 'is not something that's going to stabilize over time.'

Asked about hours/duration rules for chipping and rock crushing and the county air-quality permit requiring water-spray dust control; called the exchange 'a very constructive and meaningful exercise' and said 'we've made a lot of progress' while wanting the EAF and the reviewer's construction role nailed down.

Highlighted resident Conservation-Board geotech expert Vincent DeAnno's 'amazing experience' and pointedly asked the applicant's engineer whether its submission would change 'at all' based on DeAnno's criticism (it would not).
When invited by the chair ('Tom?') to weigh in during board deliberation, deferred with 'I don't know,' offering no substantive position on this application.

cases.name: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road
cases.applicant: J. Fane (attorney Jerry); neighbor represented by attorney George Ellison (for Barry Edelman, 88 Round Hill Road)
cases.summary: The applicant's attorney appeared without the applicant, who was unavailable, and asked to carry the continued hearing to the second January meeting to allow time to review draft approval documents with the client over the holidays. He reported the client elected to remove retaining-wall segment 'T1' entirely and submitted revised plans reflecting that. The neighbor's counsel spoke constructively, praising progress and raising administrative cleanups (drawing revision dates, papering the T1 removal, an as-built condition, a null-and-void-on-alteration clause, and whether the T2 netting should also be netted on top). The board reopened, took the neighbor's comments, and re-adjourned to January 26, 2026.
cases.publicComment: Neighbor's attorney (George Ellison, for 88 Round Hill Road) was cooperative and complimentary, offering administrative suggestions rather than opposition.

memberPositions.evidence: Expressed mild frustration that the applicant was absent and he 'wanted to get done with this application,' but accommodated the adjournment, reopened to hear the neighbor, and agreed to explore netting on top of the T2 wall.

cases.name: 263 Bedford Banksville Road (equestrian property)
cases.applicant: attorney Jerry (J. Fane)
cases.summary: An extension-of-time request for a large equestrian property with a new residence, pool/pool house, renovated exercise barn, second stable, and garage with room quarters above. Counsel explained construction is proceeding in good faith without compliance issues but cannot finish within the original 18-month window, and sought clarification that the completion deadline runs co-terminus with the building permit. The board granted a one-year extension.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to grant the extension after confirming the completion date is governed by the building permit, with no objection to the good-faith progress reported.

cases.name: 4 Vincent Lane (wetland restoration)
cases.applicant: Tom Savage; landscape architect Lewis Fusco
cases.status: public hearing closed; decision adjourned pending ARB approval of existing sheds/barn
cases.summary: A wetlands/site-plan application to modify a driveway and front walkway, remove astroturf golf areas and invasive wetland plants, and install native plantings, removing roughly 25,000 sq ft of lawn/hardscape and providing 40,000 sq ft of wetland mitigation. The Conservation Board had commended the project and the applicant addressed the town engineer's comments. The board closed the public hearing but could not adopt the resolution because two sheds and a barn built under earlier building permits never received Planning Board/ARB sign-off (a town-side glitch); it opted to send the applicant to the ARB and adopt at a later meeting without requiring the applicant to reappear.
cases.publicComment: No public spoke; Conservation Board had previously commended the project.

memberPositions.evidence: Proposed the workable path of letting the board finalize after the ARB step without dragging the homeowner back ('could we do it without the applicant even being here?... you don't have to show up'), which the chair credited as 'a good solution.'
Sympathetic to the applicants ('people... trying to do the nicest things to a property') and frustrated at the town's own oversight, steering to a low-burden ARB-then-adopt process.

cases.name: Kent Place / Verizon Parking (subdivision & site plan)
cases.applicant: Verizon / Town of North Castle (Kent Place parking expansion)
cases.status: approved (negative declaration, site plan, preliminary and final subdivision resolutions adopted)
cases.summary: A re-approval of an already-built parking expansion whose original approvals expired because Verizon never signed the plat map; no changes to what was built. A long-time abutting neighbor (Suzanne) testified at length about Verizon's chronic lack of maintenance, tree removal without replacement, an unstabilized dirt frontage with U-turns and a porta-potty, a downed fence, and unfinished screening she paid ~$40,000 to remedy herself. The board acknowledged those are largely building-department property-maintenance matters, advised her to write the building department, and re-adopted all resolutions so the plat can be filed with the health department.
cases.publicComment: Abutting neighbor (Suzanne) was strongly negative about Verizon as a neighbor - poor maintenance, tree removal, downed fence, inadequate screening - and asked for additional trees; board noted most issues fall to the building department.

memberPositions.evidence: Acknowledged the neighbor's frustration and that 'Verizon was allowed to get a pass,' but directed her to the building department for the downed fence/maintenance and proceeded with the procedural re-approval of the already-built project.

cases.name: Single-family residence & pool (Angela, applicant) - cut/fill grading
cases.applicant: Angela (owner-applicant); engineer not present
cases.status: discussion only (direction given to respond to memos and schedule a public hearing)
cases.summary: A working discussion on a hillside single-family home with a pool, garage, and retaining walls where the applicant had already reduced imported fill and wall heights and relocated the pool per prior board feedback. New wetland flagging in the rear was coordinated between the applicant's wetlands engineer and the town's consultant (Dave). The planner questioned whether setting the first floor at 473 (vs. ~470.5 garage) could be lowered to reduce cut/fill and wall grading; the board directed the applicant's professionals to answer the planner's and town engineer's memos and then set a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Worked through elevations and cut/fill with the applicant, credited her for having 'mitigated a tremendous amount' of walls and fill since the prior iteration, and pushed to answer outstanding memos and 'set a public hearing and move it along.'

cases.name: 7 Hollow Ridge Road (Wood Hollow Estates)
cases.applicant: owner/builder John Nickett; represented by Ralph Alpinsetti
cases.status: discussion only (public hearing to be scheduled; referral to ARB/RPRC)
cases.summary: A working discussion on developing a vacant 2.5-acre subdivision lot (no wetlands, sewer in the road) with a ~7,500-8,000 sq ft house comparable to neighbors, involving substantial cut and fill between a high and low grade. The planner suggested retaining walls to reduce cut, and the board explored slope steepness, a rock outcrop, and whether the design could include a walk-out basement under the current 30/38-foot height rules. The builder cited a nearly identical prior house he built on Terrace Circle; the board directed responses to the engineer's and planner's memos, a possible pre-submission meeting, and then a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Engaged constructively on the cut/fill approach, walls vs. steeper rock cuts, and encouraged pursuing a walk-out basement ('less grading, I'm all in'), steering the applicant toward scheduling the public hearing after ARB/RPRC review.

cases.name: IBM EV charging station installation
cases.address: IBM corporate headquarters campus, North Castle
cases.applicant: IBM; Seth Waltzman (representative) and colleague Stephanie
cases.status: discussion only (Level 2 to be approved at January hearing; board voted to recommend Town Board permit Level 3)
cases.summary: IBM proposed installing EV chargers in its gated, security-restricted visitor lot - three Level 2 plus one dual Level 3 fast charger - but town zoning currently limits infrastructure to Levels 1-2, so Level 3 requires a Town Board law change (a use variance being too high a bar). IBM stressed conduit run mostly above ground with minimal disturbance and no new municipal power load. The board noted a Town Board discussion on amending the EV-charger definition was already on that Wednesday's agenda, scheduled the site-plan public hearing for January, and voted to send a memo recommending the Town Board permit Level 3 charging at this gated site (which removes the highway-motorist concern).

memberPositions.evidence: Argued the gated, 24/7-manned, restricted-access location defeats the Town Board's concern about motorists pulling off the highway for fast charging, and pushed the board to formally recommend the Town Board change the law to allow Level 3.
Said 'what's in front of me right now makes all the sense in the world to put in a level three,' qualifying only that he was not privy to all the Town Board's reasons for the Level 2 cap.
Framed fast charging as 'a reasonable future use for the town,' and moved that the Planning Board send a memo encouraging the Town Board to change the law to allow Level 3 charging at this site.
Concurred with the recommendation, saying 'what Larry says makes a lot of sense.'

cases.name: 113 King Street (Toll / airport campus water tank - 'the enclave') field change
cases.applicant: applicant represented by attorney Maholic (Cuddy & Feder)
cases.summary: A field-change request after a CAD software error caused the water-tank foundation, pumping station, and generator to be built roughly 10 feet north of the approved location, with minor adjustments to spacing between the components; the generator remains six feet from the property line and everything stays zoning-compliant. With no board questions, the resolution was adopted.

memberPositions.evidence: After confirming continued zoning compliance and that the board had no questions, moved to adopt the draft field-change resolution.

cases.name: 12 Bedford Road (extension of time)
cases.applicant: owner (driveway-to-rear project, near final approval)
cases.summary: A brief extension-of-time request for a project involving a driveway to reach the rear of the property, described as very close to final approval with the applicant anxious to proceed. The board granted the extension, then closed the Planning Board for 2025.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to grant the extension of time for the near-final project before adjourning the board for the year.

themes.note: The 76 Virginia Road rock cut beside Miller Hill drove most of the meeting and most of the concern.
Impassioned public plea to protect the Miller Hill Revolutionary War battlefield and Miller House on the 250th anniversary.
Repeated worry about a 'living wall' needing perpetual maintenance and unanswered 20-50-year liability questions.
4 Vincent Lane restoration well received; new flagging coordinated on the Angela residence.
Residents cited overtaxed century-old sewer, brown well water, and rock-crushing dust at 76 Virginia Road.
Board unanimously recommended the Town Board allow Level 3 chargers at IBM's gated lot.

staffInput.summary: Active across nearly every item: pulled up plans and prior submissions; on 76 Virginia Road invoked his April 11 memo raising concern about the extensive slope removal and its threat to Miller Hill, and helped shape conditions (maintenance covenant, no-trucks-on-street, netting/ongoing-monitoring language, chipping/crushing hours); flagged the missing ARB approvals at 4 Vincent Lane; explained the 30/38-foot building-height rule at 7 Hollow Ridge; and laid out the Level 2 vs. Level 3 EV code limits and Town Board law-change path for IBM.

Carried open engineering-memo items on 76 Virginia Road and was asked to respond to the Open Space chair's EAF critique; on the single-family grading discussions signaled that detailed engineering follows once the board is comfortable with the site plan; coordinated wetland flagging with the applicant's engineer on the Angela residence.

The applicant's engineers said his comments would not change their submission.

cases.name: 4 KSL Court
cases.applicant: Property owner adding a landscaping-equipment tenant (engineer 'John' presented)
cases.summary: The applicant sought an amended site plan to add a second tenant (a landscaping equipment/vehicle storage use) to a warehouse building that had never received formal site plan approval. cases.publicComment: No public present.

Read the public hearing notice and seconded the motions to close and approve.

cases.name: 62 Nethermont Avenue
cases.address: 62 Nethermont Avenue, North White Plains (Section 122.12-5-46), R-2F zoning
cases.applicant: Owners Lindsay & Dmitry (architect Rocco Delano; applicant's father Jim New sold them the lot)
cases.summary: The applicant proposed a new ~4,865 sq ft single-family residence, positioned six feet off the south side line to preserve a future subdividable building lot. Neighbors raised concerns about rock excavation/hammering near a ~100-year-old adjoining home, house size/neighborhood character, and tree removal, while other neighbors and the applicant's father spoke strongly in support. The board debated at length whether to require protection beyond the standard chipping permit given the hammering's proximity to the neighbor. It ultimately closed the hearing and granted the resolution as amended, adding conditions that a seismic monitor be placed on the neighbor's (Pinella/'Davis') foundation and that the applicant pre-drill (line drilling) to reduce vibration.
cases.publicComment: Heavily attended. Neighbor Pinella/Penella and Nora voiced concern about rock excavation impacts, house size, and loss of neighborhood character; the applicant's father Jim New, realtor Gail Norris, and applicant Dmitry spoke in support, arguing the house is compliant and rock is limited. Tone was earnest and at times tense but not hostile; the chair explicitly urged civility.

cases.name: Short-Term Rental Law (town board referral)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Board)
cases.status: reviewed and returned to Town Board without formal comment
cases.summary: The Town Board referred its proposed short-term-rental law (a zoning-chapter amendment) to the Planning Board for input. The board discussed the framework at length: primary-residence requirement, the 30-day threshold, operating permits and building-department inspections, occupancy tax, quiet hours, and the provision barring a short-term rental on the same lot as an accessory dwelling unit (ADU). memberPositions.evidence: Argued the need to regulate is legitimate via a hotel analogy: short-term rentals lack the supervision, fire-code and safety safeguards of hotels, so the town should know where they occur; explained the ADU rationale that adding a short-term rental to a lot already carrying an accessory apartment increases intensity too much.

Read the law as the town trying to discourage short-term rentals, noting the primary-residence requirement plus the ADU restriction effectively signals 'we'd rather not'; referenced east-end-of-Long-Island 'creepy houses' and acknowledged North White concerns.

Cautioned that making the law too brief would leave openings people would exploit and make it harder to enforce; said he did not mind the law's extent/complexity and agreed with Larry that it is intended to discourage.

Said he read the law and watched the town board meeting; worried it may be too onerous/complex and could inadvertently cause noncompliance, wishing it were simpler and briefer, while agreeing its intent is to discourage short-term rentals.
