cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue
cases.applicant: Restaurant developer (offshoot of an area farm project; new investment/celebrity partners; revised exterior approved by ARB)
cases.status: extension of time granted, then flagged; variance validity referred to town attorney and ZBA
cases.summary: The applicant sought an extension of time on a previously approved restaurant site plan, reporting secured funding, an ARB-approved revised exterior, and a request tied to the new town employee parking lot. The board granted the extension, but Michael Pollack then raised Town Code Section 355-77, arguing that the ZBA parking variance (issued Dec 7, 2023) had expired after two years because no building permit or CO had been issued, and that without a valid variance there is no site plan to extend. Town attorney 'Mary' agreed there is a two-year limit and would investigate, and planner Adam Kaufman noted variances can be extended by the ZBA. The board concluded the applicant likely must return to the ZBA for a variance extension and then get re-approved by the Planning Board.
cases.publicComment: No neighbors spoke; town attorney 'Mary' confirmed the two-year variance limit and agreed to review the file.

memberPositions.evidence: Read Section 355-77 and argued the ZBA variance had expired with no building permit issued, so 'without a variance you don't have a site plan' and voting to extend the resolution 'is against the town code'; also called the ~400% parking reduction 'a problem for me.'

As chair, took the objection seriously ('I feel like we're in a predicament now'), asked the planner and attorney to confirm the two-year status, and directed that the applicant likely return to the ZBA and be re-voted, warning the attorney 'there could be some peril here.'

cases.name: 23 North Lake Road

cases.name: Cigar Membership Club (Surjon's Plaza)
cases.summary: A cigar membership club (special permit already granted by the Town Board, now in the site-plan phase) faced a parking question in the Surjon's Plaza strip mall. Adam Kaufman explained the membership-club parking code offers three standards and recommended the one-space-per-200-square-feet floor-area standard (about nine spaces), which likely avoids a variance, noting the shared lot and evening-only use. Members debated whether to use the more conservative fire-code/occupancy figure (about 17-18 spaces) as a more defensible, realistic number. The board agreed to cite a standard, made a referral to the ZBA for a parking variance if necessary, and Adam agreed to run the numbers; the submitted plan already showed 18 spaces.

cases.name: Extensions of Time — Procedure Discussion
cases.summary: Adam Kaufman opened a policy discussion on how the board handles extensions of time. The board agreed to place extensions at the top of future meetings so professionals can dispatch them quickly, while a participating professional argued the published agenda order should not bind the chair (comparing it to a courtroom). Adam also proposed adding whereas clauses to extension resolutions stating whether another board (e.g., the ZBA) had a required approval and its status, so lapses are clearly documented. The board and staff endorsed the changes.
cases.publicComment: A professional/applicant representative debated agenda-order fairness, arguing a 7 p.m. notice implies flexible ordering like a courtroom; 'Mary' called the whereas-clause idea an excellent idea.

cases.name: KEC Wetland Mitigation - Big Peninsula & Old Post Road
cases.address: Kensico River and Old Post Road (25 & 27 Old Post Road); tax lots 113.01-1-1 and 113.02-1-15/16
cases.applicant: NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP); presenter Angel Vides and full design/construction team
cases.summary: The DEP presented the wetland mitigation component of the Kensico-Eastview Connection (KEC) program, including shoreline stabilization (1,600 linear feet of rip-rap hardening), creation of roughly 2.5 acres of wetland at the Big Peninsula, and a one-acre construction staging area at Old Post Road. Construction runs fall 2026 through roughly 2029-2031 within the town's noise ordinance hours, with minimal projected traffic (about three peak-hour trucks per direction). The Conservation Board reported it had done a site walk and given a positive recommendation, and the town planner noted a thorough submission with no significant concerns. The board opened the hearing, took public comment, closed it, adopted SEQRA findings identical to DEP's, and approved the site plan, wetlands, and tree removal permits.
cases.publicComment: One resident, Zach Haas of Whipple (Whippoorwill) Road off Route 120/King Street, spoke - not opposing the project but urging traffic-safety measures at the dangerous hairpin turn where Whipple meets King Street, which he said is worsened by KEC-related commuter and construction traffic. Tone was earnest and concerned.

memberPositions.evidence: Chaired the hearing and praised the DEP's prior comparable work: the bowling-alley mitigation is an 'amazing project' that he brings people to see; glad the Conservation Board did a site walk; walked the applicant through findings and moved approval.

Read the public hearing notice; engaged the resident on the Whipple/King intersection he knows firsthand ('so I live up... I know exactly what you're talking about'), advising caution on the right turn and supporting outreach to the highway department. Supportive of the DEP application overall.

A non-chair member pressed technical questions - whether private contractors would do the work, motorist protection and egress on Route 120, the high-level objective of getting water to the UV plant, and the 27-foot tunnel diameter ('that's a lot of water'), expressing that the project is 'really amazing and impressive.'
